title: The Tractability Border of Reachability in Simple Vector Addition Systems with States
authors: Dmitry Chistikov (University of Warwick, United Kingdom), Wojciech Czerwiński (University of Warsaw, Poland), Filip Mazowiecki (University of Warsaw, Poland), Łukasz Orlikowski (University of Warsaw, Poland), Henry Sinclair-Banks (University of Warwick, United Kingdom), Karol Węgrzycki (Saarland University and MPI for Informatics, Germany)
abstract: Vector Addition Systems with States (VASS), equivalent to Petri nets, are a well-established model of concurrency. A d-dimensional VASS can be viewed as a directed graph whose edges are labeled by d-dimensional integer vectors. As a path is followed, the values of d nonnegative integer counters are updated according to these integer labels. The central algorithmic challenge in VASS is the reachability problem: can a run be made from a given starting node and counter values to a specified target node and counter values? When the input is encoded in binary, reachability is computationally intractable: even in dimension one, it is NP-hard. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive characterization of the tractability boundary for the problem when the input is encoded in unary. Our main result proves that reachability is NP-hard in unary-encoded 3-dimensional VASS, even when the structure is restricted to a simple linear-path scheme. This improves on a recent result by Czerwiński and Orlikowski [LICS 2022], in both the number of counters and the expressiveness of the considered model, and answers open questions raised by Englert, Lazić, and Totzke [LICS 2016], as well as Leroux [PETRI NETS 2021]. The underlying graph structure of a simple linear path scheme (SLPS) is merely a path with self-loops at each node. We also investigate the exceedingly weak model of computation that is SLPS with counter updates restricted to the values {-1, 0, +1}. In this case, we show that reachability remains NP-hard when the dimension is bounded by O(α(k)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function and k bounds the size of the SLPS. We complement this result by presenting a polynomial-time algorithm that decides reachability in 2-dimensional SLPS when the initial and target configurations are specified in binary. To achieve this, we demonstrate that reachability in such instances has a well-structured nature: all loops, except possibly a constant number, are either taken a polynomial number of times or nearly maximally. This extends the main result of Englert, Lazić, and Totzke [LICS 2016], who showed the problem is in NL when the initial and target configurations are specified in unary.

I. I NTRODUCTION
The reachability problem has always been of core interest in
computer science. The halting problem, which is undecidable,
is an instance of reachability from some starting configuration
in a Turing machine to some accepting configuration. Based on
a seminal (now folklore) result by Minsky [39], reachability is
undecidable in a much simpler model: two-counter machines.
This model can be seen as a finite automaton with two
nonnegative valued integer counters in which transitions can
increment, decrement, or test the counter for zero (i.e. the
transition can only be taken if a specified counter has zero
value). It is natural to consider a model without zero tests:
Vector Addition Systems with States (VASS). VASS are a
fundamental model of computation that has been studied
since the 1970s [24], [26], [27]. They are equivalent to Petri
nets, a popular and simple model of concurrency with vast
applications [3], [7], [8], [43], [44].
Concretely, a d-dimensional VASS (d-VASS) is a directed
graph with edges labelled by vectors from Zd . Vertices of
this graph are called states and edges are called transitions.
A configuration of a VASS is a state p and a vector v ∈ Nd ,
denoted p(v). Notice that vectors in the configurations are
always nonnegative, but this is not necessarily true for the
transition labels. This is because vectors labelling the transitions correspond to updates applied to counters which can
only take nonnegative values. Precisely, suppose there is a
transition from p to q labelled by u ∈ Zd , then one can
take this transition from the configuration p(v) to reach the
configuration q(v + u) so long as v+u ∈ Nd . The reachability
problem asks for a given VASS, initial configuration, and
target configuration, whether there is a sequence of transitions

from the initial to the target configuration. The dimension of
the VASS can be fixed or variable; when it is fixed, it is
specified (i.e. reachability in d-VASS vis-à-vis in VASS).
The complexity of reachability in VASS has a great history
and literature. Early on, the problem was proved to be EXPSPACE-hard by Lipton in 1976 [37] and decidable by Mayr
in 1981 [38]. More recently, the problem has amassed plenty
of attention and its complexity was finally settled: reachability
in VASS is Ackermann-complete [14]–[16], [32], [33], [36].
Finer improvements to the upper and lower bounds are an area
of active research [11], [28].
Reachability in fixed dimension VASS has also been studied earnestly. When the dimension is fixed, the encoding
of the VASS matters. Integer vectors that are transition labels can be encoded in binary (“binary VASS”) or in unary
(“unary VASS”). Reachability is NL-complete for both unary
1-VASS [42] and unary 2-VASS [21]. On the other hand,
reachability is NP-complete for binary 1-VASS (see [40,
Theorem 3.5]) and PSPACE-complete for binary 2-VASS [5].
Determining the complexity of reachability in 3-VASS, with
either unary or binary encoding, is an intriguing and longstanding problem (see, e.g., [4], [5], [16], [31]) that can be
traced back to [26]. In this paper, we present the first nontrivial lower bound for reachability in 3-VASS: we show that
reachability in unary 3-VASS is NP-hard. In fact, our lower
bound holds for an extremely restricted kind of VASS that we
will detail shortly.
Due to both its wide applicability and high complexity,
reachability has been studied for numerous variants and subclasses of VASS (for a survey on the matter, see [41]). Flat
VASS are a well-studied subclass of VASS that do not contain
any nested cycles [10], [31], [34], [35]; they characterise
semilinear reachability relations [30]. Each state in a flat
VASS belongs to at most one cycle; the underlying graph
structure can be seen as a directed acyclic graph with disjoint
cycles attached to each of the nodes. Our paper focuses on
reachability in flat VASS. Regardless of the dimension, and
even when encoded in binary, reachability in flat VASS is
in NP [13], [23]. Already in dimension one, reachability
in binary flat 1-VASS is NP-hard [25]. The complexity of
reachability in unary flat d-VASS is much more delicate. The
only known upper bounds below NP are for dimensions d = 1
and d = 2 in which reachability is in NL (this follows from
their not necessarily flat counterparts [21], [42]). Negatively
resolving questions in [5], [21], reachability in unary flat
VASS was shown to be NP-hard for dimension d = 7 [13],
subsequently improved to d = 5 [19] and d = 4 [16].
Dimension d = 3 was again left open. We close this line
of research, showing that reachability in unary flat 3-VASS
is NP-hard. Perhaps surprisingly, we prove hardness by first
restricting our systems even further, as follows.
Linear Path Schemes (LPS) are flat VASS that, informally
speaking, do not have branching. More precisely, an LPS is a
flat VASS whose underlying graph structure is a simple path
with disjoint cycles attached to the nodes. In other words,
LPS have the form α1 β1∗ α2 · · · αn−1 βn∗ αn , where each αi

and βi are sequences of transitions and the asterisk acts as a
Kleene star in regular expressions (unbounded iteration). LPS
are a basic and well-known subclass of VASS; a flat VASS can
be seen as a union of (possibly exponentially many) LPS [4],
[34]. To go one step further, we consider an exceedingly weak
model of computation: LPS with cycles of length at most
one; these innocuous VASS are known as Simple Linear Path
Schemes (SLPS) [21]. Prior to our work, it was not known
whether reachability in unary d-LPS was NP-hard, for any
fixed dimension d (and regardless of whether the LPS was
simple or not).
Overview of Results: Contributions and Techniques
Our first main contribution is the following theorem, on
(unary flat) 3-VASS. This result answers open questions on
reachability in 3-LPS [21, Section 6] and [31, Section 5].
Theorem 1. Reachability in unary 3-SLPS is NP-complete.
To show NP-hardness, we employ a combination of newly
developed and known techniques. Given an instance of 3-CNF
SAT φ(x1 , . . . , xn ), we associate, to the i-th Boolean variable
xi , the i-th prime number pi . An assignment (a1 , . . . , an ) ∈
{0, 1}n corresponds to an integer v ∈ N so that xi is true if
v ≡ 1 mod pi and xi is false if v ≡ 0 mod pi . By the Chinese
remainder theorem, for every (a1 , . . . , an ) ∈ {0, 1}n there is a
v ∈ N that encodes it: v ≡ ai mod pi for each i. Some v ∈ N
do not correspond to a valid assignment; e.g., if v ≡ 2 mod pi .
Whilst this encoding is well known, non-deterministic branching is not available in LPS (and SLPS). So, to ensure validity,
we cannot directly “say” that v ≡ 1 mod pi or v ≡ 0 mod pi
for every i. Because of this, our construction fits everything
into a conjunction (logical AND) of checks, which together
ensure that a “guessed” number v ∈ N encodes to a valid
assignment, and moreover this assignment satisfies φ.
As it turns out, it suffices to test that v ∈ N is not
divisible by an appropriately chosen small integer q, for
polynomially many values of q. This sequence of tests is
expressed as a unary 1-SLPS extended with non-divisibility
assertions (Lemma 6). Such assertions can, in turn, be realised
by a novel family of unary 2-SLPS extended with zero
tests (one 2-SLPS for each non-divisor q ≥ 2). The formal
description is in Fig. 4, and Claim 7 asserts the correctness. By
combining the 3-CNF SAT implementation with this family,
we now have a unary 2-SLPS with zero tests for which
reachability coincides with the satisfiability of φ. Importantly,
the zero tests in the 2-SLPS are heavily restricted: they only
lie on transitions between the self-loops, so there are at most
polynomially many of them.
Now these zero tests also need to be implemented. To this
end, we review the “controlling counter” technique, originally
developed in [16, Section 4]. Intuitively, this technique takes
a VASS with zero tests as input, and outputs a VASS without
zero tests. The new VASS uses an additional counter to
simulate a polynomial number of zero tests on the other
counters. In this paper, we provide a new black-box version
of the “controlling counter” lemma, which we believe is more

amenable and has wider applicability compared to the ones in
the literature. With this new Lemma 5, the proof of Theorem 1
is completed by applying it to the unary 2-SLPS with zero tests
which we constructed above.

Next, we consider what is perhaps one of the weakest
models of computation involving multiple counters. These are
VASS with constant updates in {−u, −u + 1, . . . , u − 1, u},
where u ≥ 1 is a constant independent of the size of the
VASS. If u = 1, i.e. updates can only belong to {−1, 0, 1},
we say the VASS is unitary. In general, one can construct
a polynomial size unitary VASS that is equivalent to a unary
VASS: for example, a transition with update x += 5 can be split
into five successive transitions each with the update x += 1.
Such a construction does not work for simple LPS, because a
single-transition cycle cannot be split into several transitions.
It is not at all clear if there exists a constant dimension d ∈ N
for which reachability in unitary d-SLPS is NP-hard. For our
second main contribution, we achieve one of the closest results
one could hope for.
Theorem 2. Reachability in unitary α(k)-SLPS is NPcomplete.
Here, k denotes the size of the reachability instance and α :
N → N is the inverse of the Ackermann function Ack : N →
N. Thus, the restriction to α(k)-SLPS permits the dimension
of the SLPS to grow, but only very slowly relative to the size.
We use the same approach to obtain NP-hardness: reduction
from 3-CNF SAT. We first reuse Lemma 6 since the aforementioned 1-SLPS with non-divisibility assertions is unitary.
However, we must work harder to implement non-divisibility.
We construct a unitary 5-SLPS to test whether x (the primary
counter maintaining the guessed value of the assignment)
is not divisible by q. Although it is more intricate than its
unary counterpart, the overall idea remains: add a non-zero
remainder to x and then test divisibility by q, before restoring
the original counter values. (The construction is presented in
the full version of this paper and its properties are summarised
in Claim 9.) Accordingly, we obtain a unitary 5-SLPS with
a polynomial number of zero tests for which reachability
coincides with 3-CNF satisfiability.
There is a major difference in how we simulate zero
tests in unitary SLPS. For this, we use technique known as
“multiplication triples” [16, Section 3] which was initially
proposed in [12, Section 3]. Here, three counters with initial
values b = B, c = 2C, and d = 2BC can be used to simulate
C many zero tests on other counters whose sum is always
bounded above by B. The challenge for us to overcome is
how to initialise a triplet of counters with the right values:
we need the quantity B to be at least exponential and C
to be polynomial. To do this, we manipulate some ideas, in
particular, from [28], that were used to show that reachability
in VASS is Ackermann-hard. We build a unitary d-SLPS

of size O(A(d))1 which, from an initial configuration with
counter values 0d , reaches a configuration with counter values
(0d−3 , B, A(d), B · A(d)), where B ∈ N can be arbitrarily
large (Claim 11). By setting d = A−1 (k) = O(α(k)), we
obtain an O(α(k))-SLPS that initialises a triplet of counters
with the desired values. Once this is achieved, the simulation
only requires replacing a zero test with a constant number of transitions and self-loops, which are indeed unitary
(Lemma 10).
To complement our first two results and to trace the
tractability border for reachability in unary d-SLPS from
the other side (upper bounds), we study an extension of
reachability in unary 2-SLPS where the initial and target
configurations are encoded in binary. Recall that reachability is
NL-complete in unary 2-VASS [21] and PSPACE-complete in
binary 2-VASS [5]. In these papers, the encoding of vectors in
the VASS transitions, the initial configuration, and the target
configuration are treated in the same way. A recent line of
research focuses on VASS in which the encoding of VASS is
treated differently to the encoding of source and target [18].
Namely, the VASS itself is fixed and only the initial and
target configurations form an instance of the problem. The
complexity of the reachability problem in such instances is
currently unknown but conjectured to be in PSPACE, even
for general VASS. In our result, the VASS is not fixed but,
in a similar spirit, the initial and target counter values are
encoded differently.
Theorem 3. Reachability in unary 2-SLPS is in P even if the
initial and target configurations are encoded in binary.
The proof builds on the result when the initial and
target configurations are encoded in unary [21] and introduces new techniques. Observe that, in an SLPS

Further Related Work
As mentioned above, reachability in flat VASS can be
decided in NP, even though the shortest reachability witnesses
could be exponentially long; it follows from the fact that
reachability can be expressed as an integer linear program [23].
Another example is NP membership of reachability in binary
1-VASS, where the shortest paths can have also have exponential length [25]. The proof idea is to find a positive cycle
followed by a negative cycle, which allows transitions to be
reordered freely in the middle part of the run.
In linear path schemes, the reachability problem has also
been studied with continuous semantics. In a continuous
VASS [6], the update of a transition can be multiplied by
any real number in (0, 1]. Very recently, it was proven that
reachability in continuous LPS is in P [1, Theorem 13] and
reachability in continuous 2-LPS with zero tests is NP-hard [1,
Theorem 21]. Differently from our paper (aside from the
continuous semantics), in these results transitions in VASS
and LPS are encoded in binary.

B. Constant Updates and Inverse Ackermann Dimensions
Typically, the choice of updates (the numbers occurring
on the transitions) of a VASS, or their encoding, does not
influence expressivity of the model even though that choice is
likely to influence its size. However, if we restrict our focus
to VASS subclasses, this may not be true; in this section we
consider a situation in which expressivity is influenced by the
choice of numbers on the transitions.
A VASS has constant updates if all counter updates on all
transitions belong to {−u, −u + 1, . . . , u − 1, u} for some
constant u ∈ N that is independent of the size of the VASS.
We say that a VASS is unitary if that constant is one (so
all updates belong to {−1, 0, 1}). In general, a VASS can
be simulated by a VASS with constant updates (in fact by
a unitary VASS) of the same dimension. The construction
is rather simple, for example, one can replace a transition
with an update of +5 with five transitions with updates of
+1. The size of the resulting unitary VASS is equal to the
size of the original VASS times the greatest absolute value
of any of its updates. Thus, a unary VASS can be simulated
by a polynomial size unitary VASS of the same dimension.
The same cannot be said for simple linear path schemes; the
aforementioned construction does not respect the structural
requirement that the cycles can only consist of one transition.

VI. F URTHER RESEARCH
We think that the following questions are interesting open
problems worth further research.
Theorem 2 shows that reachability is NP-hard for SLPS
already in an “almost fixed” dimension. We conjecture that
even a stronger version of this statement is true.
Conjecture 39. There exists a number d ∈ N such that the
reachability problem for unitary d-dimensional SLPS is NPhard.
In the above conjecture the term “unitary” can be equivalently changed into “fixed-updates”, as by Lemma 8 changing
a unary SLPS with fixed updates to a unitary SLPS results
only in multiplication of the dimension by a constant. This
change, however, makes a difference if we fix the dimension.
Therefore, the following is an interesting open problem. We
deliberately chose to ask it for SLPS with constant updates
instead of for unitary SLPS, as we believe that for fixed
dimension this is a more robust class of VASS.
Open Question 40. Is reachability in 3-dimensional SLPS
with constant updates in P?
Also, to extend our upper bound, it is natural to ask
whether this result extends from unary 2-SLPS to general
unary 2-VASS. We believe that the main challenge lies in first
extending Theorem 3 to unary flat 2-VASS.
Open Question 41. Is reachability in unary 2-VASS with
initial and target configurations encoded in binary in P?
